Viral Escape from Antibodies Targeting Conserved Sites

## Abstract

Influenza A virus (IAV) escape from antibody-mediated immunity causes repeated

epidemics, requiring continuous monitoring and vaccine updates. The identification of monoclonal

antibodies (mAbs) targeting conserved sites on influenza hemagglutinin (HA) has raised the

possibility of generating vaccine-elicited antibody responses that restrict IAV escape. However,

limited work has addressed how viruses may escape broadly reactive mAbs should next-generation

vaccines be widely administered. To further our understanding of IAV escape, we used deep

mutational scanning viral libraries, structural studies, and biochemical assays to characterize

escape pathways from mAbs targeting conserved sites in HA.

The development of broadly reactive mAbs is dependent on the exposure history of an

individual, intertwining virus and antibody evolution through the processes of antigenic drift and

affinity maturation. We show that affinity maturation of mAbs targeting the conserved receptor

binding site (RBS) restricts escape in the “imprinting” strain that originally elicited the mAb

lineages. However, the barrier to escape from RBS-directed mAbs is relatively low for

antigenically drifted IAVs. Amino acid positions that escaped RBS-directed mAbs are similar to

those mutated in Nature.


<!-- Page 7 -->


iv

We identified mAbs that neutralize all H1N1 or H3N2 IAVs and further engineered a pan-

H1 mAb for improved neutralization potency. Although escape mutations from pan-H1 mAbs are

rare in Nature, H1N1 viruses readily escaped pan-H1 mAbs in vitro. We structurally defined the

HA “head” and “stem” epitopes targeted by pan-H3 mAbs, which shows unique modes of

recognition compared to other mAbs. Based on these structures, we identified likely sites of escape

from these pan-H3 mAbs.

We used Ramos B cell display to affinity mature an RBS-directed mAb that was isolated

prior to the 2009 pandemic. We found that the addition of one or two amino acid mutations enabled

recognition of a post-pandemic HA but reduced affinity to a pre-pandemic HA. However, the

evolved variant maintained a high barrier to escape for the imprinting strain. These data underscore

that this RBS-directed mAb is “specialized” to the strain originally recognized by the naive

antibody.

This work identifies mechanisms by which IAVs escape mAbs targeting conserved sites

and suggests strategies for next-generation vaccine designs.

## 1. Overview

Influenza viruses evolve to escape antibody-mediated immunity, causing repeated epidemics. This

evolution is enabled by low fidelity replication of the viral genome, resulting in a diverse viral

variant population. Prior immunity then selects variants during annual infections in the human

population. The selected mutations that drive antigenic change primarily reside near the receptor

binding site (RBS) of influenza hemagglutinin (HA) as antibodies targeting these regions block

infection and are produced at high frequency within the population. Every few years, new antigenic

variants become dominant world-wide, requiring vaccines to be routinely reformulated.

Antibody responses after exposure to new antigenic variants, through vaccination or infection,

depends on individual immune histories. The first influenza strain that an individual is exposed to

influences subsequent antibody responses, a phenomenon known as immunological imprinting1-5.

After initial exposure, B cells, encoding antibodies as B cell receptors (BCRs), undergo affinity

maturation where affinity and specificity is refined in repeated cycles of mutation and selection6.

Secondary responses to new antigenic variants recall this memory B cell repertoire, updating the

BCRs through further maturation and/or differentiating memory B cells into antibody-secreting

cells. This population immunity in turn drives the antigenic evolution of influenza viruses.

Recalling memory B cells that cross-react between historical and contemporary strains can boost

responses that recognize conserved epitopes on influenza HA.

Antibodies targeting conserved HA sites can neutralize a wide range of influenza viruses.

Reconstruction of the evolutionary pathways that lead to these antibodies show that broad

reactivity is achieved through affinity maturation, consistent with immunological imprinting.


<!-- Page 17 -->


3

Next-generation vaccines often use such antibodies as templates to design immunogens aimed at

eliciting broad antibody responses7. The viral evolutionary consequences of recalling imprinted

antibodies, however, remains unexplored. Here, we review the molecular mechanisms of virus

evolution, B cell responses, antibody recognition of conserved sites, and methods used to identify

viral escape variants.

## 2. Antigenic evolution of influenza viruses

Despite widespread vaccination, seasonal influenza viruses annually infect ~10% of the global

human population, causing ~4 million cases of severe illness and approximately half of a million

deaths each year8-10. Antigenic evolution of circulating influenza viruses allows repeated infections

of the same individual. In this section, I review influenza viruses with a focus on the antigenic

evolution of HA, the predominant antibody target.

2.1 Circulating influenza viruses in humans

Influenza viruses (Orthomyxoviridae family) are enveloped and classified in four genera or types

(A-D), of which influenza A and B viruses cause human disease. Influenza A viruses (IAVs) are

responsible for pandemics caused by spillover events from avian or swine reservoirs, whereas

influenza B viruses are only known to circulate in humans9. Both influenza A and B viruses are

2.2 Generation of diversity and selection of influenza virus variants

Two mechanisms result in influenza virus diversity: antigenic shift and antigenic drift17. When

more than one influenza virus infects the same host, this creates the opportunity to generate new

viruses with a mixture of genomic segments from both viruses – a process known as reassortment9.

Antigenic shift occurs when reassortment replaces the HA with an entirely new HA for which a

population has limited or no pre-existing immunity. For example, the H3N2 pandemic of 1968 was

caused by human H2N2 virus reassortment with an avian H3 virus, rendering prior immunity

ineffective9. Once herd immunity is sufficiently high, mutations in HA and NA that escape

antibody recognition become fixed – this process is termed antigenic drift10,18,19.

The PB1, PB2, and PA proteins comprise the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) complex.

Influenza H1N1 and H3N2 RdRp complexes have low fidelity, introducing nucleotide

substitutions into the viral genome at a rate as high as ~2-3 nucleotide substitutions per replication

cycle20. After infection, a single infectious virion produces ~10-1000 infectious viral progeny and

up to ~1010 over the course of an infection21-23. The combined high mutation rate and large number

of viral progeny make it likely that an antigenic variant exists during an infection of an individual.

New antigenic variants, however, only emerge every ~2-10 years24,25. To explain this discrepancy,

models suggests that selection of an antigenic variant primarily occurs during transmission rather

than within an individual, with transmission bottlenecks as low as 1-2 infectious progeny26-29.

Thus, influenza virus evolution relies on hundreds of millions of transmission events to select for

new variants, particularly in HA10,19.

2.3 Hemagglutinin structure and receptor binding specificity

HA is the surface glycoprotein necessary for receptor engagement and membrane fusion. It is the

major target for neutralizing antibodies, and thus mutations in HA primarily drive antigenic

evolution. For a virus to enter and persist in the human population, several properties must be

acquired and retained during antigenic evolution; principally, HA must engage human receptors,

but IAVs also must overcome innate immune recognition30,31, adapt the RdRp to mammalian

cells32, and spread through airborne transmission33,34.

The homotrimeric precursor HA0 is cleaved into HA1 and HA2 by host proteases enabling

conformational rearrangements at low pH necessary for fusion of the viral and endosomal

membranes35,36. HA1 contains the globular “head” domain that binds to the receptor sialic acid

found on proteins and lipids on the surface of cells whereas the more membrane proximal region

of HA, comprised largely of HA2, is known as the “stem” and contains the fusion machinery37.

The receptor binding site (RBS) on HA1 can be divided into five non-continuous segments: the

130-, 140-, 150-, and 220-loop and the 190-helix. In the center of these segments is the shallow

RBS pocket that contains some completely conserved residues across influenza A and B viruses:

W153, H183 and Y195 (H3 numbering used throughout)37. The RBS engages sialic acid from

humans (primarily α2,6-linked) and avian (primarily α2,3-linked) differently due to the linkages

and corresponding steric changes37,38 (Figure 1.2). This enforces a receptor specificity change to

directly spillover from avian to humans. Both human and avian viruses can infect swine, however,

leading to a “mixing vessel” due to the support of avian influenza HA adaptation to human-type

receptors or dual specificity (both α2,6 and α2,3 affinity) and the potential for reassortment

between human and avian viruses39,40. This receptor binding requirement constrains potential


<!-- Page 23 -->


9

mutations that can be acquired to escape potently neutralizing antibodies, which primarily target

the RBS and its periphery.

2.4 Antibody immunodominance and sites of antigenic evolution

Elicited antibodies frequently target the same sites – a phenomenon called immunodominance43-

45. In H1 HA, these antigenic sites were classically defined as Sa, Sb, Ca1, Ca2, and Cb to denote

whether such antibodies are strain-specific (S) or cross-reactive (C) when tested for reactivity

against an antigenically drifted virus37,46,47; In H3 HA, these sites are named A-E37,48,49. Antibodies

targeting Sa and Sb (and site B), which contain the 150-loop and 190-helix at the top of the HA

head, block receptor engagement50, largely explaining why these sites undergo the most antigenic

drift. Mutations at seven positions in H3 HA primarily drive antigenic evolution in influenza

viruses, known as antigenic cluster transition positions51. Of these seven positions, six reside in

site B (145, 155, 156, 158, 159, 189, and 193; bolded positions are found in these sites). H1N1

influenza viruses prior to 2009 circulated for a shorter period of time and underwent fewer

antigenic cluster changes. However, a similar subset has been identified that drive antigenic change

in H1N1s (133a, 144, 156, 190, 193; found primarily in sites Sa and Sb)52, suggesting that

antibodies that interact with these regions are primarily responsible for antigenic change in Nature

(Figure 1.3).

2.5 Influenza viruses evolve through antigenic clusters

The magnitude of antigenic change, or distance53, can be quantified by measuring the cross-

reactivity of serum elicited by one virus against other viruses using hemagglutination inhibition

(HI) assays, which measure the ability to block virus receptor engagement on red blood cells. Prior

work mapped the antigenic changes for influenza A and B viruses by combining HI data from a

large panel of infected ferret sera with genetic analyses24,25,51. These data demonstrate that

influenza viruses, particularly H1N1 and H3N2, evolve through periods of minimal antigenic


<!-- Page 26 -->


12

changes followed by large jumps or transitions to new “clusters”24,25,51, necessitating vaccine

updates (Figure 1.3). A model of influenza virus evolution suggests that this “epochal” evolution

can be explained by acquiring neutral mutations that alone may not escape herd immunity but can

change the escape effect of other mutations such that when combined, there are large antigenic

changes54. This phenomenon, the non-additive effects of mutations, is known as epistasis.

2.6 Intragenic and intergenic epistasis in influenza virus antigenic evolution

There are two general forms of epistasis that can influence antigenicity of influenza HA and NA,

which can both potentiate and constrain evolution59. The first, intragenic epistasis, is the

dependency of one mutation on the specific context or background of the rest of the protein.

Mutations that compensate for an otherwise deleterious mutation, known as compensatory

mutations, allow access to expanded mutational space that can provide escape from antibodies.

Mutations in H1 HA that cause escape from antibodies targeting the RBS pocket, Sa antigenic site,

or stem sometimes require compensatory mutations to maintain functional fitness60-62; these are

examples of positive epistasis. Epistatic interactions also regulate the accessible mutations in the

H3 HA antigenic site B63. Similarly, a mutation that causes oseltamivir (an NA inhibitor) resistance

lowered viral fitness but became widespread due to the inclusion of a compensatory mutation in

NA that restored fitness64. Additionally, combinations of mutations that cause neutral functional or

escape effects can, when combined, escape monoclonal antibodies65. Constraints, however, can

also form. A clear example of this is the demonstration that historical strains, but not more

contemporary strains, tolerate the reversion of a mutation (E190D)66. This mutation contacts

sialylated glycans and resides in the RBS. Thus, HA loses the ability to mutate this residue over

time, limiting access to potential escape mutations from antibodies that engage the RBS.

The second form of epistasis, intergenic epistasis, refers to the dependency of a mutation on the

context of another protein. For influenza, there is a functional balance between the receptor binding

protein, HA, and the receptor destroying enzyme, NA67. In theory, if an escape mutation in HA

changes receptor avidity, NA can adjust by increasing or decreasing catalytic activity to maintain

the balance. Experimental work showed that the HA mutational landscape is dependent on the


<!-- Page 29 -->


15

catalytic activity of NA65,68. Further, influenza viruses have been characterized that primarily use

NA as the receptor binding protein, though HA is still required for fusion69-71, allowing propagation

of viruses with an HA that does not bind sialic acid71. In extreme cases, mutations in HA can adapt

for the complete loss of NA by lowering receptor avidity72. Thus, the epistatic interactions between

HA and NA can regulate the mutations acquired during antigenic drift. In contrast to studying

epistasis of host proteins, viral proteins, such as HA, are highly constrained by antibodies that

shape the mutational landscape, which is driven by B cell responses to infection or vaccination.

## 3. B cell responses to antigenically drifted influenza virus variants

The widely variable exposure histories of individuals from infection(s) and vaccination(s) shapes

the antibody response that drives antigenic evolution of influenza viruses. In this section, I review

how exposure history in the context of B cell imprinting can influence the antibody response.

3.1 Immunological imprinting: Original antigenic sin, antigenic seniority, and back-boosting

In the 1930s, the first human patient-derived influenza virus was isolated and used to infect

ferrets73, demonstrating a filterable agent caused influenza illness and could be transmitted to an

animal. As influenza virus evolved in the human population, new antigenically distinct viruses

were isolated. In the 1950s, Thomas Francis Jr. and colleagues collected sera from human cohorts

in different age groups and performed a series of HI assays using the donors’ sera with

antigenically distinct influenza viruses4,74-77. Serum inhibition of influenza viruses was highest

against the strain that circulated during the donors’ childhoods (I refer to this as the imprinting

strain), though inhibition was also observed for more contemporary strains. When the serum was

adsorbed by the imprinting strain, the inhibitory responses against more contemporary strains were


<!-- Page 30 -->


16

greatly reduced or completely absent4 (but not vice versa; adsorption with the contemporary strain

had minimal effect on the inhibitory response to the imprinting strain), suggesting that antibodies

elicited by recent exposures largely boosted antibodies that were cross-reactive between the strains

(Figure 1.4A). Thomas Francis Jr. created the term “original antigenic sin” to describe this

phenomenon that antibody titers are highest against the first infecting strain (the imprinting

strain)4,74-76,78. It was proposed, however, that vaccination with multiple strains may leave an

imprinted antibody response with broad reactivity that could be boosted with subsequent

exposures, thus converting original antigenic sin to “an initial blessing of induced immunity”78.

The “antigenic seniority” model has refined the concept of original antigenic sin5. Antigenic

seniority further adds that there is a hierarchy of reactivity to antigenic variants – neutralizing

antibody levels are lower as a function of increasing antigenic distance from the imprinting strain5.

One mechanism that supports antigenic seniority is “back-boosting”, which describes the

observation that exposure to contemporary strains boost responses to historical strains. Combining

sera from infected donors of differing age groups at multiple time points across a large scale

showed that infection back-boosted antibody titers with the largest response (change in titer from

pre-infection) towards the infecting strain, but steady-state titers remained highest to the imprinting

strain, consistent with antigenic seniority79 (Figure 1.4B).

One interpretation of original antigenic sin or antigenic seniority (which we refer to more generally

as imprinting from here on) is that successive exposures to antigenically distant strains could be

exploited to generate more broadly reactive responses targeting conserved sites. To better

understand imprinting, we must consider the underlying mechanisms of the B cell responses.

3.2 Naive B cell repertoire

Antibodies, encoded initially as membrane-bound BCRs, are assembled from recombination of

heavy chain variable (V), diversity (D), and joining (J) genes and light chain V and J genes80,81,

forming a tetrameric protein with two heavy chain and two light chain copies. Addition of non-

templated nucleotides between the V-D and D-J junctions in the heavy chain generates further

diversity82,83. This accumulates a paired chain diversity of possible BCRs estimated at ~1016-1018

that is orders of magnitude higher than the number of circulating B cells (~109)84. During early B

cell development, the rearranged BCRs are subjected to selection to ensure productive BCRs and

limit autoreactivity. After passing these checkpoints, naive B cells migrate to secondary lymphoid

organs (e.g., lymph nodes and spleen). Prior to secreting antibody that can bind viral antigens, B

cells go through additional selection processes.

3.3 Initial exposure and affinity maturation

After infection or vaccination, BCR recognition of the antigen triggers internalization through

endocytosis. Processing (proteolytic degradation of the internalized antigen into peptides) and

presentation (loading peptides into major histocompatibility complex class II) enable these B cells

to engage primed CD4 T cells, which in turn activates the B cell. Activated B cells either

differentiate to short-lived antibody secreting cells (plasmablasts) or migrate towards the follicular


<!-- Page 33 -->


19

dendritic cells to seed germinal centers (GCs) where the affinity of the BCR is further refined

through a process known as affinity maturation85,86. Initial antigen affinity of a naive B cell

influences the expansion and differentiation to extrafollicular plasmablasts or GC B cells; high

affinity biases B cells to become antibody secreting cells without entering GCs87,88. Once the GC

B cells form two distinct regions termed the dark zone (DZ) and light zone (LZ), the process of

affinity maturation begins.

GC B cells express high levels of the enzyme activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) that

converts cytidine to uracil in the variable regions of the BCR6. Depending on the imperfect DNA

repair processes that attempt to fix the mismatch (base-excision repair or mismatch repair),

mutations at and adjacent to the site of deamination can occur89. In the absence of DNA repair

processes, replication of the C>U mutation will result in C>T or G>A mutations89. These

nucleotide mutations may result in amino acid mutations in the BCR that alter the affinity and

specificity. GC B cells with mutated BCRs enter the LZ where competitive, affinity-based

acquisition of antigen from follicular dendritic cells dictates the fate of the B cell90. B cells with

high affinity BCRs acquire more antigen, which in turn leads to more antigen presentation to T

follicular helper cells that signal to continue affinity maturation by returning to the DZ or to

differentiate into memory or antibody-secreting cells6,90,91 (Figure 1.5A,B). GCs export memory

B cells earlier compared to plasma cells and typically harbor fewer somatic mutations92. Despite

affinity-dependent selection, germinal centers formed after immunization with complex antigens

(e.g., influenza HA) maintain low affinity BCRs93. After influenza virus infection, GCs can last

for long periods of time (~6 months), continuously recruiting new B cells into GCs94-96 and

exporting GC B cell graduates as effector B cells with refined affinity and specificity. Phylogenetic


<!-- Page 34 -->


20

reconstruction of clonal lineages can recapitulate the trajectory of affinity maturation, allowing

inference of the naive and intermediate B cell receptor sequences97,98 (Figure 1.5C).

A recent study demonstrated that a large portion (~95%) of memory B cells encode BCRs with

weak or undetectable affinity towards the immunizing antigen102. The proposed explanation is that

memory B cells largely prepare for exposure to a related, but new variant (e.g., an escape mutant).

Earlier work demonstrated this possibility by showing that memory B cells derived from infection

could bind a viral escape mutant, but long-lived plasma cells were specific for the wild-type

virus103. Thus, such memory B cells generated by the first influenza virus exposure, in addition to

new naive B cells, form the basis for secondary immune responses to antigenically drifted

influenza viruses.

3.2 Secondary B cell response to influenza virus

Secondary responses are complicated due to variable factors such as immune history, antigenic

distance between exposures, and antibody feedback. Thus, studies are still ongoing to elucidate

the mechanism(s) that shape secondary responses. Memory B cells derived from the initial

exposure can re-enter secondary GCs for further affinity maturation or differentiate to plasmablasts

to rapidly secrete antibodies100,101,104,105 (Figure 1.5A,B). Studies in mice showed that prime-boost

immunizations rarely recruit memory B cells to secondary GCs105 and memory B cells mostly

differentiate directly to antibody-secreting cells in the context of heterologous infections104. In

humans, however, influenza vaccination produces GCs with a high proportion (up to ~90%) of GC

B cells derived from memory, though with significant variability across donors101.

Only a few, memory-derived clones make up the secondary plasmablast response to influenza

vaccination, peaking one week after vaccination100 (Figure 1.5B). The magnitude of this memory-

derived plasmablast response is associated with increased HI titers106. This oligoclonality is


<!-- Page 38 -->


24

consistent with studies directly measuring the clonal diversity in serum after vaccination, showing

that only ~1-10 clonotypes make up most of the polyclonal antibody response, often drawing from

the pre-existing repertoire107,108. Thus, despite the enormous diversity of the naive B cell repertoire,

only a few antibody clonotypes, largely derived from memory B cells, directly act to block

transmission of influenza viruses in an individual thereby pressuring for viral escape.

Circulating antibody from pre-existing immunity inhibits the recruitment of B cells into secondary

GCs in an epitope-specific manner by blocking antigen uptake (epitope masking)109. Antibody

epitope masking then enables B cells targeting previously untargeted epitopes to gain an

advantage. In the context of influenza, as HA antigenic drift or shift lowers pre-existing immunity

towards variable sites. This, in theory, supports the activation of memory B cells targeting those

sites that retain affinity to the drifted strain. These memory B cells can then re-enter GCs to

undergo additional rounds of affinity maturation or differentiate into plasmablasts. Thus, exposure

to antigenically distinct strains has the potential to elicit a B cell response that targets conserved

sites (Figure 1.5B).

In response to the antigenic shift that occurred during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, people born

between ~1983-1996 produced a dominant antibody response towards the conserved RBS when

exposed to the pandemic strain55,110. Sequential exposure in ferrets recapitulated these findings,

identifying that a residue shared between the pandemic strain and seasonal influenza strains (1983-

1996), K133a in the RBS was primarily responsible for this effect55. In general, the first exposure

to the H1N1 pandemic boosted not only RBS-directed antibodies, but also those toward a


<!-- Page 39 -->


25

conserved site on the side of the HA head111,112. Several reports have also shown that vaccination

with non-circulating H5 or H7 HAs boost memory B cells targeting conserved sites113-116.

Sequential exposure to antigenically drifted viruses can also activate B cells targeting conserved

sites. Isolation of plasmablasts induced by vaccination with a 2006 H1N1 strain showed that many

of these plasmablasts produced antibodies targeting the conserved RBS pocket117,118. Antibody

lineage reconstruction of these RBS-directed antibodies showed that the unmutated common

ancestors (UCAs), representative of the naive antibody, only bound to strains that circulated around

1990, which was when the donor was born3. The mature antibodies, however, bound all strains

that circulated from 1990 to 2007, including the vaccine strain3. These data have two major

implications: 1) exposure to HAs from distinct antigenic clusters can boost B cell responses

targeting conserved epitopes and 2) B cells targeting conserved sites evolve breadth during affinity

maturation. Antibodies imprinted by previous exposure, however, often have higher affinities

towards the initial antigen rather than the contemporary antigen111,119-121. While some imprinted

antibodies provide protective benefits120, a remaining question is how these antibodies influence

escape. While further affinity maturation and boosting of antibodies targeting conserved,

functional sites may restrict viral escape mutations, antigenically drifted viruses may enable

additional routes of escape due to epistatic effects from previously acquired mutations.

4.1 Stem-directed antibodies

Most of the current next-generation vaccine design efforts for influenza aim to elicit antibodies

that target the stem region131-135. These stem antibodies function by (1) blocking the cleavage of

HA0 into HA1 and HA2, which is required for infection, and/or (2) preventing the conformational

rearrangement that fuses the viral and endosomal membranes136. The appeal of stem antibodies is

the breadth of reactivity, though the neutralization potency is typically weaker compared to

antibodies targeting the head. Stem antibodies that bind all group 1, all group 2, or even all known

influenza viruses122,128-130,137,138 have been identified, leading to the notion of generating so-called

“universal” influenza vaccines.

Clinical evaluation, however, of prophylactically or therapeutically administered stem antibodies

suggest these antibodies provide minimal protection, even in the case of prophylactic

administration with the most broadly reactive stem antibody that was further engineered in vitro

for enhanced affinity128 and extended half-life (NCT05567783). All clinical trials of stem

antibodies have not progressed to Phase 3. The amount of antibody provided in the prophylactic

trial is similar to the amount of head-directed antibody found in human sera139, suggesting that

even if vaccination could convert the serological response to a completely stem-directed response,

this approach may ultimately fail. In part, this is likely because stem antibodies require Fc-

dependent effector functions (e.g., antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity) to impart protection

in mouse models137,140, demonstrating that although these antibodies show neutralization in vitro,

they do not neutralize in vivo.


<!-- Page 43 -->


29

Eliciting stem antibodies through vaccination may not overcome the protective threshold required

for these antibodies106. Consistent with this, stem antibodies have been found to be widely

prevalent in human sera (~80% of people contain stem-specific antibody titers)141, but do not select

for viral escape mutations in Nature despite the ability to do so in vitro62,142-144. Conservation then

appears to be largely due to inadequate concentrations of stem antibody in sera required for

immune pressure. Although stem antibodies may have an important role in mitigating the severity

of infection upon pandemic occurrences, high vaccine efficacy against circulating influenza

viruses require sterilizing protection, which these stem antibodies do not afford confer. Although

head-directed antibodies do not confer the same level of breadth compared to stem antibodies, they

provide better protection in humans145.

4.2 Receptor binding site-directed antibodies

The most potent influenza virus neutralizing antibodies described to date target the HA RBS,

blocking receptor engagement required for cell entry. CH65 is a prototypic RBS-directed antibody

isolated from plasmablasts one week after vaccination117, which engages the conserved RBS

pocket by mimicking sialic acid interactions13. Structural characterization of several additional

antibodies from the same donor, derived from diverse V gene usages, identified that a shared

dipeptide motif mimics sialic acid contacts118. The receptor mimicry of these antibodies affords

broad reactivity spanning ~30 years13,146. Several groups have identified RBS-directed antibodies

from many donors against multiple subtypes58,124,147-153. Due to the variability surrounding the RBS

and the footprint size of an antibody, RBS-targeting antibodies have limited breadth across

subtypes or groups, underscoring a tradeoff between neutralization potency and breadth.

Nevertheless, immunogen design efforts154,155, including ours156-158, aim to elicit antibodies


<!-- Page 44 -->


30

towards the RBS in the effort to increase protective efficacy compared to current vaccination.

However, RBS antibodies engage the periphery of the RBS that contains immunodominant

epitopes. Thus, although RBS antibodies are highly potent, they are susceptible to antigenic drift.

4.3 Antibodies targeting the lateral patch and vestigial esterase domains

Structural studies of neutralizing antibodies that do not engage the RBS have identified additional

conserved epitopes on the side of the HA head that have no specific function. Antibodies that target

these epitopes, the lateral patch and vestigial esterase domains, function by inhibiting viral

attachment and/or egress111,112,125,126,159 and are broadly reactive only within a specific subtype.

Exposure to the pandemic 2009 H1N1 virus boosted antibodies that target the lateral patch, but

subsequent viral evolution added an N-linked glycosylation that prevented binding of many, but

not all antibodies targeting the lateral patch111,112. Upon further exposure to post-pandemic viruses

through vaccination, lateral patch antibodies were found in plasmablasts at frequencies

approaching zero111. Thus, lateral patch antibodies constitute a low fraction of the existing antibody

repertoire in sera, contributing to the continued conservation of this epitope. The creation of mosaic

nanoparticles that display the HA head domain from multiple strains showed the capacity to elicit

antibodies towards the lateral patch, providing a broadly reactive antibody response160.

Nanoparticle vaccination in humans has also elicited broadly reactive antibodies against H3

viruses targeting the vestigial esterase domain161, but thus far no lateral patch or vestigial esterase

antibodies have been identified to bind all H3 HAs. Furthermore, although lateral patch antibodies

have pan-H1N1 neutralization activity, there is little information on influenza virus escape from

these antibodies. If new vaccination strategies aim to elicit antibodies targeting these conserved

sites, we should identify the epitopes and evaluate escape potential.


<!-- Page 45 -->

4.4 Non-neutralizing epitopes: head and head-stem interface

Several recent reports have identified broadly reactive epitopes at protomer interfaces (head and

head-stem interfaces) that are occluded in the pre-fusion form of HA and thus do not

neutralize156,162-166. Although head interface-directed antibodies do bind cell surface HA, they bind

weakly compared to a stem antibody, poorly bind to virions164, and bind the uncleaved HA0

precursor better than the cleaved, active HA162. Thus, although these antibodies have broad

reactivity, they have suboptimal properties compared to stem antibodies, which seem to provide

minimal protection against seasonal influenza viruses in humans.

## 5. Experimental approaches to select viral escape mutants

Broadly reactive antibodies are often used as tools to aid in developing next-generation vaccines

aimed at eliciting similar antibodies7 or as standalone prophylactics or therapeutics. However, it is

unclear how the virus will evolve if the repertoire predominantly includes these types of these. In

this section, I briefly review experimental approaches to select for viral escape variants from

monoclonal antibodies.

5.1 Traditional passaging approaches

Traditional approaches use the natural diversity generation of influenza viruses to generate mutant

libraries. Antibodies can then be added to select escape mutations from these viral populations

during virus passaging using cell lines, eggs, or animal models. For in vitro experiments, there are

two general approaches: 1) adding antibody near or completely neutralizing antibody

concentrations to select for single escape mutations already present in the initial virus population

and 2) adding partially neutralizing concentrations of antibodies, which can be increased during


<!-- Page 46 -->


32

successive passages. In both approaches, the selected variants are those most accessible by single

nucleotide substitutions from the wild-type nucleotide sequence which is perhaps more reflective

of the mutations that may arise in Nature. In the second approach, repeated passaging may also

select for multi-mutant variants not found in the original viral diversity. The limitation of these

traditional passaging approaches, however, is the inability to comprehensively evaluate many

amino acid mutations, particularly those that require more than one nucleotide substitution.

5.2 Deep mutational scanning approaches

To comprehensively identify escape mutations from monoclonal antibodies, the technique of deep

mutational scanning (DMS)167,168 has been applied to influenza viral proteins60,63,66,142,169-176,

including HA. In this method, amino acid positions across an entire protein, region, or selected

sites are mutated to all other 19 amino acids in a DNA library. Reverse genetics approaches177 can

then generate infectious influenza virus DMS libraries. After applying a selection pressure (i.e.,

passaging and/or addition of antibody), next-generation sequencing quantifies the enrichment of

selected variants compared to the input library or control. Passaging the virus library in the

presence of antibody can thus identify escape mutations.

These systems have provided invaluable information detailing escape mutations for influenza, but

also many other viruses178-181. However, these studies often use viruses no longer present in the

human population (e.g., A/WSN/1933) or viruses that are not reflective of the exposure history of

a particular antibody lineage. Furthermore, due to the inability to sample very large sequence

space, efforts aimed at addressing epistatic effects between residues are limited to selection of a

few amino acid positions63,66. Recent reports using a smaller, non-viral protein and modeling


<!-- Page 47 -->


33

suggest that an alternative method, termed phylogenetic DMS, can quantify epistatic changes of

individual mutation182,183. In this system, DMS libraries are generated in multiple backgrounds

derived from phylogenetic reconstructions, enabling the effect of a mutation to be compared

between backgrounds to determine epistatic effects. Thus far, similar approaches in viruses have

been limited to evaluating changes in functional effects of the SARS-CoV-2 spike184,185.

## 6. Conclusion

Here, I have reviewed the molecular basis of both influenza HA and antibody evolution. These co-

evolutionary forces have implications for designing next-generation vaccine design to elicit

antibodies targeting conserved sites. However, how viruses evolve to escape recognition of such

antibodies has not been studied. In this thesis, I create viral DMS libraries to characterize escape

from antibodies targeting conserved sites specifically focusing on the HA head. In Chapter 2, we

determine viral escape from imprinted antibody lineages in the imprinting and drifted virus

backgrounds. These data show that affinity maturation limits the number of escape pathways, but

antigenic drift enables multiple escape pathways. In Chapter 3, we describe isolation of pan-H1

and H3 antibodies that target the HA head and stem, engineer the pan-H1 antibody for increased

neutralization potency, and assess viral escape. We additionally structurally characterize the

epitopes targeted by the pan-H3 antibodies. In Chapter 4, we engineer Ramos B cells to express

and evolve an RBS-directed antibody. Using these engineered cells, we affinity mature an RBS-

directed antibody to recognize a strain not previously encountered. These data show that acquiring

affinity to a new strain can be achieved but at the expense of affinity to historical strains. In Chapter

5, we summarize our findings and highlight remaining unanswered questions.

## ABSTRACT

Viruses evolve to escape host humoral immunity by acquiring mutations in surface glycoproteins

that subsequently abrogate antibody affinity – a process called antigenic drift. An initial virus

exposure can imprint antibody responses such that the identity of the imprinting strain influences

future responses to drifted strains; this is well-characterized for anti-influenza immunity. When

recalled by infection or vaccination, imprinted antibodies targeting the influenza virus

hemagglutinin (HA) cross-react with drifted influenza strains and often engage conserved sites on

the globular HA “head”. Imprinted antibodies typically have lower affinity for drifted strains, but

considerable breadth. It is unclear how antigenic drift influences viral escape pathways from

imprinted antibodies. Here, we selected clonal lineages from two human donors that target the

conserved receptor binding site (RBS) and lateral patch epitopes to assess viral escape pathways

from historical H1N1 viruses that include the likely imprinting and drifted viruses. Using deep

mutational scanning we show that although affinity maturation of imprinted antibody lineages

restricts escapability in the imprinting strain, there are abundant escape routes in the contemporary,

drifted strain. We find that antibody affinity maturation eliminated approximately half to all single

amino acid escape mutations in the imprinting strain. However, in a drifted strain we find that

despite similar neutralization potencies, the number of escape mutations from these imprinted

antibodies increases from ~0-2 to ~34-45 mutations, suggesting that although antibody affinity

maturation can afford breadth, recognition also remains biased towards the imprinting strain.

Structural characterization of an escape pathway provides a mechanism of how affinity maturation

can overcome viral escape and antigenic drift can expand the number of escape pathways. These

results show that one mechanism by which influenza virus can continually evolve in the human

population is recalling imprinted antibodies that subsequently allow for more escape pathways.

## INTRODUCTION

Influenza viral escape from host humoral immunity induced by prior infection or

vaccination reduces vaccine effectiveness, requiring annual updating1. To escape host humoral

immunity, influenza acquires mutations in the surface-exposed hemagglutinin (HA) that evade

antibody recognition while also maintaining functional fitness. This antigenic drift of seasonal

H1N1 and H3N2 influenzas primarily occurs in the HA head domain, which is responsible for

engaging the receptor sialic acid. Every ~2-10 years, these mutations result in major antigenic

changes in circulating influenza A viruses (IAVs) resulting in a new antigenic “cluster” that

reduces the efficacy of prior immunity2-4. Notably, only a few amino acid positions around the HA

receptor binding site (RBS) are largely responsible for these antigenic cluster transitions2-6.

Modeling IAV evolution suggests that periods of minimal antigenic change followed by

antigenic cluster transitions can be explained by accumulation of “neutral” mutations that do not

substantially alter antigenicity alone but change the effects of subsequently acquired mutations7;

mutations that precipitate antigenic cluster transitions are thus dependent on the context of HA.

One experimental study reinforces this “epochal” evolution model by demonstrating that a single

mutation can have no effect in one IAV strain, but after acquiring additional mutations, the same

mutation results in complete escape from monoclonal antibodies8. This dependency of a mutational

effect on a particular background IAV strain or the presence of other mutations (epistasis) prohibits

accurately predicting the effects of single mutations. To better understand how mutations might

impact IAV escape from monoclonal antibodies, including those that target the RBS9-12, deep

mutational scanning (DMS) approaches have been used, which introduces a large number of

mutations into a library, typically “scanning” every selected position with all possible single amino

acid changes. When applying different selection pressures (e.g., antibody escape), the change in


<!-- Page 69 -->


55

frequency of these mutations can be quantified by next-generation sequencing. These studies found

that different IAV strains can have different barriers to escape11 and epistasis between mutations

in the RBS can influence escape12. However, previous DMS reports of escape from anti-head

antibodies used a historical IAV (WSN/1933) and primarily mouse antibodies, which does not

accurately reflect the complex immune history that occurs in humans.

The immunological imprinting phenomenon – first termed “original antigenic sin”13-15 –

describes that antibodies found in sera generated from the initial IAV exposure are largely “back-

boosted” and refined by subsequent exposure to antigenic variants rather than generating de novo

antibody responses. A related concept known as “antigenic seniority” demonstrates that antibody

titers are higher for IAVs more antigenically like the imprinting strain; titers are gradually lower

for IAVs that have undergone an increasing amount of antigenic drift. Recent murine studies

showed that the degree of back-boosting versus de novo responses is dependent on the antigenic

distance between the HAs16. Larger antigenic distances between the first exposure (i.e., imprinting

strain) and the boosting strain (i.e., drifted strain) increase the proportion of de novo responses and

elicits serum antibodies targeting drifted epitopes by preventing previously circulating antibodies

from blocking those sites16,17. In humans, infection with IAVs broadly back-boosts antibodies with

the greatest increase in titer towards the infecting strain, while steady-state, long-lived antibody

titers remain biased towards the imprinting strain18.

Boosting imprinted antibody responses can increase antibody titers and further refine

specificity towards conserved sites. Imprinting by an IAV initially engages naive B cells

recognizing HA before undergoing rounds of somatic hypermutation and selection in germinal

centers (GCs) to generate a pool of memory B cells encoding antibodies with high affinity and

specificity for a particular epitope, a process known as affinity maturation. Subsequent exposure


<!-- Page 70 -->


56

to antigenically drifted IAVs primarily activates these memory B cells that either re-enter GCs for

further affinity maturation to the altered epitope or directly differentiate into antibody secreting

cells (e.g., plasmablasts)19,20. By sequencing antibody variable regions from plasmablasts isolated

after influenza vaccination, clonally related antibodies can be identified and through

phylogenetically reconstruction the unmutated common ancestor (UCA) and intermediates in

affinity maturation, inferred21-26.  Isolation and structural characterization of several RBS-directed

antibody lineages showed that these antibodies have sialic acid-like contacts, resulting in

significant breadth due to RBS conservation21,25,26. Notably, the UCAs of these RBS-directed

lineages only bound HAs from the antigenic cluster that circulated around the time the donor was

born, but the mature antibodies could recognize strains from multiple clusters, spanning up to ~30

years24. These RBS-directed lineages along with knowledge of the likely imprinting and boosting

IAV strains allows interrogation of how affinity maturation influences viral escape at a

functionally conserved site and whether the barrier to escape changes in the boosting, drifted strain

due to epistatic effects.

Here, we use deep mutational scanning and viral escape assays in multiple H1N1 strains

from different antigenic clusters to understand viral escape in the context of imprinted antibody

lineages. We find that although affinity maturation in these lineages greatly increases the barrier

to escape in the imprinting strain, antigenically drifted strains readily escape these antibodies

despite similar neutralization potencies. This strain dependency is due to epistasis between

mutations that individually have no impact on escape, which supports IAV evolution models.

Importantly, we find that escape selections with only two RBS antibody lineages identifies

positions responsible for major antigenic cluster changes in IAVs, suggesting such RBS-directed

antibodies may drive viral evolution in Nature on the global level. Surprisingly, these data suggest


<!-- Page 71 -->


57

that recalling imprinted antibody lineages through vaccination, even those that are broadly

neutralizing by targeting a conserved site, has a lower barrier to escape. Thus, next-generation

influenza vaccines must consider how drawing from immune memory may simultaneously provide

protection and generate an antibody response with many escape pathways.

## RESULTS

Imprinted antibody lineages targeting conserved HA sites

The RBS and lateral patch are conserved epitopes on the HA head and are targets of

monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that are neutralizing across multiple antigenic clusters (Figure

2.1A). While RBS conservation is imposed by functional constraints (e.g., receptor engagement),

the lateral patch has no defined function23. Prior work isolated mAbs from human donors post-

vaccination and reconstructed lineages that target the RBS or lateral patch to determine the UCAs

and identify the likely imprinting strains21-26 (Figure 2.2A). The RBS-directed mAbs were isolated

from day 7 plasmablasts of a donor born in 1989 after vaccination in 2008, which contained the

IAV strain A/Solomon Islands/03/2006 (SI06)22. The lateral patch-directed mAbs were likewise

isolated from plasmablasts of a donor born in 1975 after vaccination with a 2009 pandemic strain23.

A common feature of these lineages is that the UCAs recognize a single antigenic cluster that

corresponds to the likely imprinting strains that circulated near the donors’ birth23,24. The RBS-

directed UCAs bind to IAVs that circulated ~1989 whereas the lateral patch-directed UCA binds

to IAVs that circulated ~1977. Affinity maturation of these linages enabled the mAbs to bind

distant antigenic clusters, consistent with an imprinted antibody response (Figures 2.1B and

2.2A).


<!-- Page 72 -->


58

To evaluate viral escape in both the imprinting and drifted IAVs from the inferred UCAs and

affinity-matured mAbs, we selected RBS-directed and lateral patch-directed lineages and three

H1N1 strains from distinct antigenic clusters2. The RBS-directed lineages, 641, 643, 652, and 860,

were likely imprinted by an IAV similar to A/Siena/10/1989 (SN89) as the UCA binds this IAV

but not IAVs from other antigenic clusters; the affinity-matured RBS-directed mAbs additionally

bind SI06. The lateral patch lineage, 6649, was likely imprinted by an IAV similar to

A/USSR/90/1977 (USSR77) as the UCA has affinity for this HA but not SN89 or SI06. However,

affinity-matured lateral patch-directed mAbs can bind USSR77, SN89, and SI06. We therefore

selected USSR77, SN89, and SI06 IAVs as they represent likely imprinting strains and the change

in reactivity breadth during affinity maturation of these lineages (Figures 2.1B and 2.2A).

Viral library generation and experimental design

We generated viral libraries in three different background IAV strains, USSR77, SN89,

SI06, containing all single amino acid mutations and deletions within the HA head (positions 52-

263, H3 numbering) (Figure 2.1C). Each viral library is barcoded after the stop codon to link

individual mutations through long-read sequencing, facilitating downstream sequencing (Figure

2.2B). To avoid potential RBS adaptation mutations to cell lines expressing avian-type receptors,

we used humanized MDCK cells, which have only α-2,6 linked sialic acid, and mimics the human

upper respiratory tract28. For each virus background, two independent libraries were generated and

selected separately (Figure 2.3). To enhance the genotype-phenotype linkage after viral library

generation, we passaged the libraries at a low MOI such that each virion displays a single antigenic

variant (Figure 2.3). After the low MOI passage, we sequenced the resulting library and calculated

functional scores29 for each amino acid variant by determining the change in frequency, relative to

wild-type, between the plasmid and viral libraries (Figures 2.2C and 2.3). Functional scores

derived from independent passaging of biological replicates correlated (r ~ 0.4-0.8) (Figure 2.2D).

To assess viral escape from our selected antibody lineages, we performed 18 deep

mutational escape selections, each in biological replicate using independently generated libraries

(Figure 2.3), using the UCA or mature mAbs from each lineage against the imprinting or drifted

strains (Figure 2.1C). We analyzed the data with three main metrics: (1) the change in the number

of escape mutations; (2) the change in the barrier to escape at each position; (3) differentially

selected mutations between selections (Figures 2.1C and 2.3).

Viral escape in the imprinting strain is restricted by affinity-matured RBS antibodies

We tested the neutralization potency of the UCA and mature mAbs from the five lineages

against the imprinting strains. All mature mAbs more potently neutralized the imprinting strains

(Figure 2.4A). The UCAs from RBS-directed lineages 860, 652, 641 completely neutralized SN89

virus (Figures 2.5A, 2.5F, and 2.5K), allowing us to compare the identity and number of escape

mutations between the UCA and their respective affinity-matured mAbs.

We used 10x the IC99 mAb concentration for selections with the mAb present during the

initial infection to select large-effect escape mutations to RBS-directed mAbs and to apply a

consistent neutralization pressure across selections. We used differential selection9 to quantify the

enrichment of escape variants and normalized each selection to its maximum value, assuming

maximally selected variants completely escape mAb neutralization. We define the number of

escape mutations as those with relative escape of >0.5 in two independently selected biological

replicates – in other words, these mutations were reproducibly positively selected with at least half

the differential selection value of the most highly selected mutation when applying a completely

neutralizing concentration of mAb (Figure 2.3). Due to the number and scale of selections we

performed, it was impractical to perform each selection at multiple antibody concentrations, which

aids in predicting the change in neutralization potency29,30. Instead, here we focus on large-effect

mutations by the addition of a completely neutralizing concentration of mAb.

We found 7-18 escape mutations from the UCAs of RBS-directed lineages. In contrast to

the UCAs, we found 0-7 escape mutations from the affinity-matured RBS-directed mAbs, reducing

the number of escape pathways by up to 100% and eliminating escape at certain positions (Figures

2.4B-2.4C). SN89 escaped UCA860 with 15 mutations at positions 133a, 159, 189, and 193

including acidic residues Glu and Asp, as well as a deletion at 133a (Figures 2.4B-2.4E). However,


<!-- Page 82 -->


68

affinity maturation of UCA860 to CH65 abrogated the effect of these mutations on viral escape,

and we were unable to select for any escape mutations from CH65 (Figures 2.4C and 2.5A-2.5E).

Similarly, SN89 escaped UCA652 with mutations at positions 133a, 145, 159, 190, and 193, but

the two affinity-matured mAbs H2227 and H1244 completely eliminated escape at positions 133a,

145, and 159 and reduced the total number escape mutations at the remaining two positions

(Figures 2.4C, 2.4F, 2.4G, and 2.5F-2.5J). We observed similar findings for lineage 641; the

affinity-matured mAbs reduced the number of possible escape mutations (Figures 2.4C, 2.4H,

2.4I, and 2.5K-2.5O).

Notably, despite using the same amount of neutralizing mAb in each selection, relative

escape values between selections may not necessarily be directly comparable as an escape

mutation could partially reduce affinity to one mAb while reducing affinity of another mAb to

undetectable levels. To test how relative escape compares with affinity, we next recombinantly

expressed selected SN89 variants as HA trimers to determine affinities to the UCAs and affinity-

matured mAbs (Figure 2.5U); we found a rank correlation between fold change in affinity and

relative escape values (ρ = 0.78) (Figures 2.5U and 2.5V). Affinity-matured mAbs maintained

wild-type affinities against mutations that otherwise reduced affinity of the corresponding UCAs

by over 100-fold (Figure 2.5U). Presumably due to the use of 10x the IC99 for each mAb in each

selection, the selected mutations showed a binary response where most (~88%) of mutations

defined as “escape” mutations reduced affinity to undetectable levels and those not defined as

“escape” mutations did not alter affinity (Figure 2.5W). These data show that affinity maturation

of RBS-directed mAbs restricts the number of viral escape pathways, raising the barrier to escape.

Antibody tilting eliminates escape potential in the imprinting strain

To understand how an affinity-matured mAb restricts viral escape, we determined crystal

structures of UCA860 bound to MA90 (an SN89-like imprinting strain) and CH67 bound to

MA90-G189E, which escapes the UCA860 but not affinity-matured CH65 or CH67 (Figure

2.6A). Superimposing UCA860:MA90 and CH67:G189E complexes shows that the escape

mutation G189E directly clashes with the CDRL3 of the UCA860 (Figures 2.6B and 2.6C). In

the CH67:G189E complex, the variable domains “tilt” towards the 130- and 150-loops of the HA

by ~10°, allowing the CDRL3 to shift ~3 Å away alleviating the steric clash (Figures 2.6B and

2.6C). Our prior work identified that somatic mutations N52H and G31D, which occurred early

during affinity maturation24,26, compensate for the escape mutation G189E31. In the CH67:G189E

structure, these residues engage the 150-loop of HA, providing new stabilizing contacts to tilt away

from the distant clash with G189E (Figures 2.6B and 2.6C). Despite this tilting, the CDRH3 with

the critical dipeptide that mimics sialic acid is similarly positioned within the RBS, providing an

anchor point. Thus, somatic mutation that enables formation of new stabilizing contacts distant

from the escape mutation can prevent escape by allowing the antibody to tilt away from the site of

escape.

Viral escape mutations from imprinted antibody lineages are abundant in drifted strains

To examine how escape differs between an imprinted and drifted IAV strain, we next

determined the escape profiles of the mature mAbs from RBS-directed lineages 860 and 652 using

SI06, as well as the lateral patch-directed lineage 6649 against SN89 and SI06 (Figure 2.7). In

general, mAbs neutralized the drifted strains with lower potency compared to the imprinting strain,

however, affinity-matured mAbs from lineages 860 and 652 maintained similar neutralization

potencies (< 5-fold change) (Figure 2.7A). Compared to escape in the imprinting IAV strain, we

observed an increase of 10-43 escape mutations for affinity-matured mAbs from lineages 860 and

652, despite this modest change in neutralization potencies (Figure 2.7B). In lineage 860, CH65

less potently neutralized SI06 compared to SN89 by 4.5-fold, but SI06 escaped with a larger

number of mutations (0 in SN89 vs. 34 in SI06) (Figures 2.7B, 2.7C, and 2.7E). The positions in

SI06 that escape CH65 are those that SN89 used to escape UCA860 but with a higher number of

mutations (Figures 2.7C, 2.4C, and 2.8A-2.8E). Similarly in lineage 652, mature mAbs H2227

and H1244 neutralized SN89 and SI06 equivalently, but SI06 escaped using many possible

mutations (2 in SN89 vs. 35-45 in SI06) (Figures 2.7B, 2.7C, and 2.7F). The positions conferring

escape from H2227 and H1244 in SI06 are the same as those observed for SN89 with UCA652

(Figures 2.7C, 2.4C, and 2.8F-2.8J). In the lateral patch-directed lineage, we observed a

progressively lower barrier to escape in IAVs that drifted away from the imprinting strain from

USSR77 to SN89 to SI06 (Figures 2.7B, 2.7D, 2.7G, and 2.7H). Not only did more mutations

appear, but more mutations at additional positions (e.g., positions 128, 166, and 171) escaped mAb

neutralization (Figure 2.7D, 2.7G, 2.7H, and 2.8K-2.8O).

To confirm these results, we generated a panel of 28 recombinant HAs with observed

escape mutations in different IAV backgrounds to assess affinities (Figure 2.7I).

Mutations G189D and A193F/K/D had no effect on CH65 affinity for the imprinting strain (SN89),

but reduced affinity to undetectable levels in the drifted strain (SI06) (Figure 2.7I). Similarly,

mutations D190Q/I and A193F/D abrogated binding of H2227 and H1244 only in the context of

the drifted strain (SI06) (Figure 2.7I). Although we were unable to select for SI06 escape variants

in this assay using lineage 641 due to low neutralization potency, affinity of some variants selected

by other RBS antibodies (e.g., A193F/D) had no effect in SN89, but abrogated binding in SI06

(Figure 2.7I).

The lateral patch-directed lineage had distinct differences between clonally related

members Ab6649 and Ab9207 (Figures 2.7I and 2.8K-2.8O). For both mAbs, mutations

K166L/A had no effect on affinity to the imprinting strain (USSR77). However, these mutations

significantly reduced Ab9207 affinity in the context of SN89 whereas Ab6649 retained affinity. In

the further drifted strain, SI06, the same mutations now abrogate Ab6649 affinity. Mutation

Thr173 escaped neutralization by both Ab6649 and Ab9207 (Figure 2.8O) and introduces a

predicted N-linked glycosylation site, which is similar to a previously identified natural escape

mutation in this epitope23.

Members of lineages 652 and 641 also selected for escape mutations that were not shared

between affinity-matured mAbs of the same lineage. In lineage 652, the mutation S145R in SI06

escaped H1244 and reduced affinity, but this mutation had no impact on H2227 affinity (Figures

2.7I and 2.8J). In lineage 641, mutations G189D and G159E abrogated binding affinity to H1270,

but not H1261 (Figure 2.7I). These data show that there are more escape pathways possible from

imprinted antibody lineages in the drifted IAV strain compared to the imprinting IAV strain; the

result is a lower barrier to escape an oligoclonal antibody response for drifted strains compared to

the imprinting strain (Figure 2.9).

The changes in escape and affinity by a single amino acid mutation in different background

multiple mutations might explain these changes, we compared the sequences and structures of the

imprinting strain (SN89 or MA90) with that of the drifted strain (SI06). Notably, two mutations in

the RBS occurred during natural evolution from SN89/MA90 to SI06: a deletion of Lys at residue

133a (∆K133a) and E156G. In the UCA860:MA90 structure, the CDRH3 residues E102 and P103

interact with K133a and residues Y109 and Y111 interact with E156 (Figure 2.10A); thus

evolution of SN89/MA90 to SI06 with mutations ∆K133a and E156G removes these critical

contacts within the antigen combining site (Figure 2.10B). Based on the UCA860 interacting with

these two residues, we hypothesized that binding of CH65 and CH67 to HA bearing G189D (which

abrogates affinity only in SI06) is contingent on the contacts with either K133a and/or E156. To

test this, we generated SI06 containing the escape mutation G189D with or without reverted

mutations +K133a and/or G156E, and measured affinities by ELISA (Figure 2.10C). Only when

both residues were present did lineage 860 members bind this variant with wild-type affinity

(Figure 2.10C). Thus, epistasis between mutations at 133a or 156 with 189 enable escape when

no single amino acid in the imprinting strain escapes the CH65.

We next passaged MA90 virus with increasing concentrations of CH67 to allow for

multiple mutations to accrue. The resulting virus had a mixed population of E156K, A193D, and

N158D (Figure 2.10D). We assayed affinity to recombinant HA variants alone or in combination.

Alone, the mutations did not affect binding of CH67, but when E156K and A193D were combined,

a ~200-fold affinity loss occurred and was further impacted with N158D (Figure 2.10D). Thus,

there appears to be an epistatic effect with mutations at 156 and 193 enabling viral escape from

## DISCUSSION

In this study we find that affinity maturation reduces the possible number of escape

mutations, but antigenic drift enables multiple escape pathways from imprinted antibody lineages

targeting the RBS and lateral patch (Figure 2.11). The increase in escape mutations in drifted

strains is not restricted to a particular lineage or epitope, as we find similar conclusions regarding

escape from lineages that target distinct epitopes, use different variable germline genes, and are

isolated from different donors. Moreover, we find that boosting imprinted antibody lineages can

yield potently neutralizing antibodies in agreement with a study demonstrating antibodies with

original antigenic sin phenotypes can contribute to protective responses32. Our data, however,

suggests that boosting imprinted antibodies increases the number of escape routes in a hierarchical

manner for increasingly divergent strains, consistent with antigenic seniority.

The influenza-specific serum repertoire after vaccination is oligoclonal with only ~1-10

clonotypes representing most of the serum19,33. We tested antibodies from four RBS lineages

isolated from a single individual25, suggesting escape from an oligoclonal RBS antibody response

may look like what we report here. The positions selected from only two RBS-directed lineages

overlap with the residues known to drive antigenic change in IAVs3,5,6 (133a, 144, 145, 155, 156,

158, 159, 189, 190, 193; bolded positions overlap), and mutations at these positions almost

exclusively account for escape from these RBS-directed lineages. These data suggest that recalling

imprinted antibody lineages targeting the RBS may drive natural evolution more than previously

thought and escape from such antibodies may be able to predict antigenic clusters that are yet to

emerge.

The HA stem is currently a major target for so-called “universal” vaccine candidates,

despite the clinical failure of prophylactic administration of the most broadly reactive and further

engineered stem-targeting antibody (NCT05567783). The UCAs of two broadly reactive stem-

directed antibodies, CR9114 and FI6, only bound group 1 HAs and acquired group 2 HA reactivity

through affinity maturation34,35, similar to our observations with the lineages described here. When

assaying for escape using deep mutational scanning in H1N1 or H3N2 viruses, escape was difficult

for H1N1 (group 1), but readily occurred for H3N2 (group 2)11. Thus, even for anti-stem

antibodies, the escape barrier appears to be high in the imprinting strain, but not the strain the

lineage gains reactivity to through affinity maturation. This is not unique to IAV as epistatic effects

in SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain also modulate whether mutations escape

neutralization36. These data suggest that recalling imprinting lineages with subsequent affinity

maturation may universally increase the number of mutations accessible for escape.

The changing effect of single amino acid mutations in one IAV background compared to

another highlights how significantly the background context influences the barrier to escape. For

example, CH65 has no single amino acid escape mutations in SN89 but acquiring only one or two

mutation(s) (∆K133a and/or E156G) that by themselves has no effect enables a change from no

escape mutations to a possible 35 mutations that can completely escape recognition. These data

are consistent with the “neutral network” model of influenza epochal evolution7 that suggests

acquiring mutations that themselves do not result in antigenic change can facilitate large antigenic

change upon acquiring a second mutation.

This “switch-like” regulation from few to many escape pathways by minimal antigenic

drift may inhibit the ability to predict how a virus may evolve in response to novel immune

pressures elicited by next-generation vaccines or monoclonal antibody therapies. Computational


<!-- Page 108 -->


94

methods aimed at predicting viral evolution require knowledge of existing evolution (i.e.,

naturally-occurring sequences)37,38, but the goal of many vaccination approaches is to change the

dominant immune pressure by focusing antibody responses to conserved epitopes. Here, however,

we show that escape from RBS antibodies select similar positions as those currently acquired on a

global level.

Monoclonal antibodies derived from recall frequently have the highest affinity for the

imprinting strain32,39,40, as is the case for lineage 86031. Consistently, despite similar neutralization

potencies between SN89 and SI06, affinity-matured mAbs from imprinted lineages 860 and 652

retain the highest barrier to escape in the imprinting strain. These data suggest that affinity

maturation in these lineages biases both affinity and the barrier escape towards the imprinting

strain, “committing” antibody recognition to a historical HA. However, because affinity

maturation to antigenically drifted variants has the potential to increase the barrier to escape, next-

generation vaccine design should focus on immunizing with a priori predicted or experimentally

determined antigenic clusters rather than attempting to “guide” affinity maturation towards

conserved epitopes41 through sequential vaccination using historical strains. Future studies should

also investigate the barrier to escape from de novo versus recall antibody responses.

Limitations of study

Although the levels of somatic hypermutation in RBS antibodies described here suggest

multiple rounds of affinity maturation24, it is unknown whether these antibodies indeed underwent

affinity maturation towards SI06 or a SI06-like strain. Vaccination with SI06 may have recalled

memory B cells directly to plasmablasts42. Therefore, it may be possible that further affinity

maturation additionally restricts potential escape mutations in SI06. In addition to epistasis within


<!-- Page 109 -->


95

HA, intergenic epistasis between HA and NA also influences the accessible escape mutations in

HA43,44. For each virus library, we used the matched NA from that strain. Thus, differences in NA

may also play a role in the mutations that are selected for escape. We used mAbs isolated from

day 7-8 plasmablasts of two donors. Although these mAbs contributed to the short-lived

plasmablast response, it remains to be shown whether this effect is similar in the long-lived plasma

cell compartment.

Virus library design

Viral libraries were designed to cover all single amino acid mutations in the HA head

domain (positions 53-263, H3 numbering) of three H1N1 virus strains: A/USSR/90/1977

(USSR77, EPI230599), A/Siena/10/1989 (SN89, EPI171157), A/Solomon Islands/03/2006 (SI06,

EPI155197). A known egg adaptation mutation in SI06 (Q226R) was reverted to Q226.

Rather than sampling all codon mutations, we used the most frequently used codons from

influenza A viruses from > 40,000 coding sequences in the Kazusa database46 (Table S1). This

reduced nucleotide diversity of the library and ensured comparison of codon changes between

strains was not due to effects caused by specific codon usage. Because cloning into the reverse

genetics vector uses the BsmBI restriction enzyme (see below), in the rare cases that the selected

codons introduced a new BsmBI site, we modified the surrounding nucleotides such that

introduction of a codon never introduced a new BsmBI site. Additionally, these codons did not

introduce SalI restriction sites, which was used to linearize the cloned plasmid libraries prior to

long-read sequencing (see below). In addition to non-synonymous mutations, we also aimed to

introduce synonymous and stop codons at a frequency of ~1-2% of the library to provide a measure

of fitness. Every fourth position was mutated to a stop codon in the head and nonsynonymous

codons were added wherever wild-type did not match the selected codon usage from the Kazusa

database.

To facilitate simplicity in downstream PCR reactions of many selections in different viral

strains, we incorporated a barcoded region directly after the stop codon, similar to a barcoding

strategy used in H1N1 influenza viruses previously47. Here, however, we incorporated two

barcodes separated by a cloning scar. Immediately after the stop codon are defined barcodes. The

first four nucleotides of this 12-nucleotide barcode define a particular background virus (virus


<!-- Page 112 -->


98

barcode), and the latter eight nucleotides define which position is mutated at that position (position

barcode). Both virus and position barcodes have a hamming distance of 3 or greater to prevent

sequencing errors from misassigning barcodes, which was achieved using BARCOSEL48. These

defined barcodes were added during PCR generation of the library (Twist Bioscience). During

cloning (see below), a random 12-nucleotide barcode was added after a four base pair scar

immediately after the defined barcodes. Following the random barcodes is a repeated 80 nt packing

sequence as previously described47,49. The C-terminal region of the coding sequence was modified

as previously described to prevent a repeat packing signal47, and the nucleotide sequence of the

barcoded region was made consistent between all strains such that the primer binding sites enable

amplification of the barcoding regions of all three strains (plasmid maps can be found at

https://github.com/dpmaurer/imprinted_ab_escape). Linear double stranded DNA libraries with

this design were ordered from Twist Bioscience.

HA library cloning

We first generated a modified version of pHW200027 where we replaced the stuffer

sequence with a GFP cassette (pDM_RG068) (plasmid maps can be found at

https://github.com/dpmaurer/imprinted_ab_escape). Bacterial colonies carrying these plasmids

fluoresce green under blue light, allowing us to quantify the proportion of colonies carrying

undigested plasmid after cloning. We used a three-piece golden gate cloning50 method to assemble

the HA coding sequence library (Twist) and a DNA segment encoding the random 12-nucleotide

barcode and repeated packing sequence (IDT) with the pDM_RG068 backbone. The linear DNA

libraries were delivered in plates where each well contained variants at one given position. For

each library, we resuspended each well in 5 µl of water and pooled 2 µl from all wells. Although


<!-- Page 113 -->

in theory golden gate cloning does not require pre-digestion of the library or plasmid, we found

cloning was most efficient when we digested the library and plasmid with BsmBI-v2 (NEB,

#R0739L) (but not the barcode fragment due to the quantity) and purified these fragments by gel

extraction prior to assembly. The three fragments were quantified by Qubit (ThermoFisher) and

combined in a plasmid : library : barcode fragment ratio of 1:2:2 or 30:60:60 fmol. BsmBI-v2

golden gate assembly mix (NEB, #E1602S, 1.2µl) and the supplied T4 DNA ligase reaction buffer

°C (20 min). The reaction was dialyzed by filling a Petrie dish with water, placing a piece of 0.025

µm filter paper on top, and pipetting the 12 µl reaction on top of the filter paper. The dialysis was

and split equally in half to generate two replicate libraries (some volume loss is expected). For

electroporator using the preset E. coli protocol (2mm cuvette, 2.5 kV). After electroporation, E.

coli transformations were recovered with 4 ml of the supplied media at 30 °C for 1 hour. The

°C for 24 hours. Then, colonies were counted and a goal of ~100,000-200,000 colonies were

scraped into 200 ml of LB with carbenicillin and grown for an additional 2 hours at 30 °C prior to

maxi prepping the plasmid DNA (Macheregy-Nagel, #740414.50).

To titer or test neutralization against viral libraries, we used a standard ELISA-based

microneutralization assay55 with some modifications. hCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates

(Corning, #3595) at 20,000-30,000 cells per well in flu media. The next day, virus was prepared

in half-log dilutions (for titering) or at 200 TCID50 / 50 µl (neutralization) in flu media containing

2 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin. For viral neutralization assays, we used the viral libraries from replicate 1

Flu media (titering) or four-fold antibody dilutions (neutralization) were added to the viruses (1:1

ratio) and incubated at 37 °C / 5% CO2 for 1 hour. The media was then removed from the cells and

virus (tittering) or virus-antibody mixtures (neutralization) were overlayed on the hCK cells. After

1 hour at 37 °C / 5% CO2, the inoculum was removed, the cells were washed with PBS, and fresh

flu media containing 1 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin was added. ~18-20 hours later, the media was

removed, cells were washed twice with PBS, and fixed with ice-cold 80% acetone in PBS for 10

minutes. After removing the fixative and air-drying, the plates were washed with wash buffer (PBS

+ 0.3% Tween20 (Sigma, #P1379)) three times before adding antibody diluent (PBS + 0.1%

Tween20 + 1% BSA) to block. After blocking for 1 hour at room temperature, the plates were

#MAB8258, 1:4000 each) in antibody diluent were added for 1 hour at room temperature. After

washing three times, a dilution of anti-mouse antibody HRP conjugate (seracare, #5220-0339,

1:20000) was added for 1 hour at room temperature. After washing five times, Ultra TMB was

added (ThermoFisher, #34028) for ~15 minutes). The development was stopped by addition of 2M

sulfuric acid before reading at 450 nm (SpectraMax).

was performed in quadruplicate or eight replicates. Neutralization potencies were determined by

subtracting background from cell only controls and normalizing 0% neutralization to the virus only

were then determined by IC99 = (99/(100-99))(1/hill slope) x IC50.
